title: Jeff Gordon kicks off Freedom 250 weekend with first individual race win in 10 years
content:
WASHINGTON — Jeff Gordon was once known as the “Wonder Boy” back when he piled up victory after victory in a Hall of Fame racing career.

Now a graying 55-year-old, it turns out Gordon’s still got it.

Gordon won the International Race of Champions’ first official event in 20 years, kicking off Washington, D.C.’s Freedom 250 weekend on the 1.7-mile street course built around the National Mall.

Fans roared as Gordon did a celebratory burnout in front of the grandstands while others in an expected Saturday crowd of approximately 70,000 stacked themselves three- and four-deep along the fence to catch a glimpse. The IROC victory marked the four-time NASCAR champion’s first individual race win since 2015 in a NASCAR Cup Series event at Martinsville Speedway — though he was also part of a team that won the 2017 Rolex 24 at Daytona sports car race.

“This is super special,” Gordon said. “It’s a real honor to be a part of this event. All of us are super appreciative to be here and see what this is like this weekend.”

Two decades ago, IROC pitted drivers from various racing disciplines against one another in identically prepared cars, but the series lost funding and concluded its run in 2006. NASCAR Hall of Fame crew chief Ray Evernham, who wrenched cars for Gordon during his prime, resurrected the series this year with cars from that era.

The series served as a support race for the Freedom 250 Grand Prix this weekend — the IndyCar event that will take place Sunday afternoon.

Gordon had one previous IROC win — in 1998 at Daytona International Speedway — but this one was particularly meaningful for a driver who retired from full-time racing more than a decade ago and is now the vice chairman of the Hendrick Motorsports NASCAR team.

“The dog has still got some bite in him,” said NASCAR Hall of Famer Kurt Busch, who finished second in the overall race.

IROC held a pair of 10-lap races using the original cars from that era (not many are left), and Gordon drove a silver No. 24 owned by Rick Hendrick from the back in both races to sweep the day.

“This is such a blast to be on the track with this group of drivers,” Gordon said. “It’s going to be hard to wipe this smile off my face for a very long time.”

Evernham told drivers in their pre-race meeting to take it easy at the start.

After all, these are original IROC cars from the early 2000s — high-dollar collector cars that essentially serve as museum pieces. They were prepared with updated parts to race again, but a crash would be disastrous.

“You weren’t taking it easy!” Gordon told four-time Indianapolis 500 winner Helio Castroneves after he saw Castroneves make bold moves at the start of the first race.

Gordon ultimately will go down as the weekend’s first winner, but Sunday’s IndyCar race marks the big prize in one of American motorsports’ highest-profile events in years.

IndyCar owner Roger Penske had Penske Corp. president Bud Denker attempt to get Congressional approval to stage a race on the National Mall and surrounding areas for America’s 250th birthday, but it fell through in a gridlocked Congress.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy then paved the way for an executive order from President Trump, which cleared the red tape and allowed the event to take place. IndyCar is said to be paying more than $35 million to hold the race, which is the first motorsports event around the National Mall.

“I felt like I was racing in an M&M’s bowl of candy with all the colors and buildings,” Busch said. “This is a monumental privilege to race on these streets.”
